We have mass spec: m/z 179.0946 (intensity 100) as base peak. Likely molecular ion? The formula? Let's compute possible formula for m/z 179.0946 (monoisotopic). Use typical elements C, H, N, O. Let's approximate: C10H13NO2 has monoisotopic mass: C10=120.000, H13=13.101, N=14.003, O2=31.989 => total 179.093. Yes matches. So molecular formula C10H13NO2.

Carbon NMR peaks: 166.40 (likely carbonyl C=O, maybe ester or amide). Others aromatic ~129-131 (multiple aromatic carbons). 52.24 (maybe O-CH3 or O-CH2). 43.47, 38.60 (aliphatic CH2/CH). So structure likely aromatic ring with carbonyl attached (ester or amide) and some aliphatic side chain.

Mass spec isotopic pattern shows M+1 at 180.0978 (approx 6% natural abundance). So single nitrogen (adds 1.003). Good.

We need propose SMILES. Use formula C10H13NO2. Could be methyl phenylacetate with amide? Let's think.

Carbonyl at 166 ppm suggests ester carbonyl (C=O of ester ~165-175). Amide carbonyl similar. Aromatic ring 6 carbons ~129-131. So aromatic ring present.

Aliphatic carbons: 52 ppm (likely O-CH3). 43 and 38 maybe CH2-CH2 attached to N? Could be N-CH2-CH2-? Let's compute: If we have methyl ester of anilide? Example: acetanilide (C8H9NO) has carbonyl ~170, aromatic ~130, CH3 carbonyl ~23. Not match.

Our formula C10H13NO2: maybe methyl 4-methylbenzoate? That's C9H8O2? Actually methyl benzoate C8H8O2? Wait: methyl benzoate C8H8O2? No, C8H8O2 is C8H8O2 (mass 136). Not.

C10H13NO2 could be methyl 4-aminobenzoate (p-aminobenzoic acid methyl ester) = C9H9NO2? Actually p-aminobenzoic acid (C7H7NO2) plus methyl = C8H9NO2? Not.

Let's compute: aromatic ring C6H4 plus substituents. Need total C10. So aromatic ring plus 4 more carbons. Could be phenylacetonitrile? That's C8H7N? Not.

Consider structure: N-methyl-4-methoxybenzamide? That would be C9? Let's count: benzamide C7H7NO, plus N-methyl adds CH3 => C8H9NO? plus methoxy? Not.

Our formula includes two oxygens, one nitrogen. Could be an amide (C=O + N) plus a methoxy group (O-CH3). That matches carbonyl (166) and O-CH3 (52). Aromatic ring 6 carbons. Additional carbon maybe CH2 linking? Let's think of N-methyl-4-methoxybenzamide? That would have OCH3 attached to aromatic (methoxy) not O-CH3 attached to carbonyl. But O-CH3 attached to carbonyl (methyl ester) would be OCH3 carbon at ~52 ppm (yes). So we have methyl ester. Then nitrogen attached to carbonyl? That would be amide, but carbonyl can't have both OCH3 and N? That's carbamate (urethane). Example: methyl phenylcarbamate: O=C(OC)NPh. Formula: C9H9NO2? Let's count: phenyl (C6H5), carbonyl carbon (C), OCH3 (C1H3O), N (no carbon). Total C8? Wait: phenyl C6, carbonyl carbon C1, OCH3 carbon C1 => total C8? Actually phenyl C6, carbonyl carbon C1, OCH3 carbon C1 = C8. plus maybe extra substituent on N? Not.

Our formula C10 suggests phenyl (C6) + carbonyl carbon (C1) + OCH3 (C1) = C8, need two more carbons maybe on N as ethyl? N-ethyl? That would add C2H5. So N-ethyl carbamate: O=C(OC)NCC? That would be C9? Wait: O=C(OC)NCC: carbon count: phenyl C6, carbonyl C1, OCH3 C1, ethyl C2 = C10. Yes matches. So structure: phenyl carbamate with ethyl on nitrogen and methyl ester OCH3. That's methyl phenylcarbamate ethyl? Actually O=C(OC)NCC? But N attached to ethyl (CH2CH3). So SMILES: O=C(OC)NCCc1ccccc1? Wait phenyl attached to carbonyl carbon? In carbamate, phenyl attached to carbonyl carbon? Actually phenyl carbamate: O=C(OC)NPh (phenyl attached to N). But we have phenyl attached to carbonyl carbon? Let's think: O=C(OC)NCC? The phenyl is attached to carbonyl carbon? Not; carbonyl carbon attached to O (ester) and N (carbamate). The phenyl could be attached to N (as N-phenyl). So N-phenyl ethyl carbamate? That would be O=C(OC)N(Cc1ccccc1)CC? Wait N attached to phenyl and ethyl? That would be N-phenyl-N-ethyl carbamate (dimethyl?). But we have only one nitrogen, two oxygens, and 10 carbons. If N attached to phenyl (C6) and ethyl (C2) that's 8 carbons plus carbonyl carbon (1) plus OCH3 (1) =10. Yes.

So SMILES: O=C(OC)N(CC)C1=CC=CC=C1? Actually N attached to phenyl and ethyl: N(ethyl)(phenyl). So SMILES: O=C(OC)N(CC)c1ccccc1. Let's check carbon count: phenyl C6, ethyl C2, carbonyl C1, OCH3 C1 =10. Hydrogens: phenyl H5 (since attached to N), ethyl H5 (CH2CH3), OCH3 H3, carbonyl none, N maybe H0. Total H =5+5+3=13. Yes matches C10H13NO2. Good.

Now check carbon NMR: carbonyl carbon ~166 ppm matches. Aromatic carbons ~129-131 (six). OCH3 carbon ~52 ppm matches. Ethyl carbons: CH2 attached to N ~38-43 ppm (makes sense). CH3 attached to CH2 ~? maybe 13 ppm but not observed; maybe overlapped with aromatic? Not listed. The carbon NMR list includes 43.47 and 38.60, likely CH2 and CH3? But CH3 would be ~13 ppm, not present. Maybe the CH3 is not observed due to low intensity? But we have only 10 carbons, we have 9 peaks listed: 166.40, 131.87, 129.70 (x2), 129.01 (x2), 129.00, 52.24, 43.47, 38.60. That's 9 peaks, but we have 10 carbons. Some aromatic carbons overlapping (multiple same values). The CH3 carbon maybe overlapped with aromatic? Not likely. But maybe the ethyl is CH2-CH3, CH2 at 38.6, CH3 at 13 not listed maybe due to low intensity or overlapping with something else. Could be missing.

Nevertheless plausible.

Let's validate SMILES: "O=C(OC)N(CC)c1ccccc1". Validate.
